Article Title: At 10, she lost her grandmother to breast cancer; at 17, Dubai teen Saiyette Aima built an AI platform and took cancer awareness to India
Article Text:
Beginning of an effort

Awareness work in India

CareCheck : An AI platform

At 10, Saiyette Aima could not understand the medical language around breast cancer. But its consequences were clear to her from the get-go. Her grandmother was diagnosed with Stage 3 disease after noticing a small, pimple-like mark on her neck, she began chemotherapy and radiation and the family quickly entered a period of treatment and uncertainty. While she was thousands of miles away from her grandmother in Delhi, the experience stayed with her. Now, cancer was no longer a disease she read about on paper, it was a part of her life. “I watched her go through chemotherapy and radiation and saw how cancer affected not just her health, but our entire family,” Saiyette told Khaleej Times.Her grandmother later died in 2020, during the Covid-19 pandemic, when travel restrictions made the event even harder for the family. “My parents, my sister and I were the only people in our family that lived here in Dubai. The rest of my family lived with her in Delhi,” she said.A few years later, the Dubai College student cut her locks and donated them through Locks of Hope, a Friends of Cancer Patients programme that provides wigs for people undergoing chemotherapy. “Hair loss is such a visible part of treatment for many patients, and it felt like a simple, practical thing I could do,” said the now 17-year-old.“It was a small gesture, but it taught me that I don’t have to wait until I have a large platform or extensive resources to begin helping,” she added. This marked just the beginning of her initiative for bettering the lives of cancer patients.Aima launched For Her, For Hope, a fundraising campaign through YallaGive. While she initially aimed to collect Dh5,000 by approaching her school, family, friends and community, the final amount exceeded Dh10,400 and earned her recognition as YallaGive's Fundraising Hero of the Month. The money supported Pink Caravan, the Friends of Cancer Patients initiative that promotes awareness and offers free screenings.A perceptive and dedicated teenager, Aima soon realised that a single campaign could only help so much. She then created Pink for Purpose, a cancer-awareness initiative.Many people had questions they felt uncomfortable asking and complex medical terminology only made the information difficult to absorb. Thus, she expanded Pink for Purpose into a YouTube channel featuring oncologists and other specialists discussing warning signs, screening, treatment, inherited risks, recovery and the emotional effects of cancer. The conversations also improved her own understanding of the truly life-changing disease. Treatment varies widely among patients; its effects may continue through physical symptoms, and people may also face reduced confidence, fear of recurrence and uncertainty within families. “Cancer can affect almost every part of a person’s life,” she said.Her conversations extended to include educational sessions and magazine content with IntelliJelly, which published her writing and featured an awareness video.The most direct phase of her advocacy took her to India, where she helped organise free awareness and screening camps with doctors from AIIMS New Delhi and the National Cancer Institute in Jhajjar. Conversations with 150 attendees exposed her to numerous practical barriers: uncertainty about bodily changes, limited opportunities to ask questions, and health advice obscured by language or terminology. “Giving someone health information is only useful if they can actually understand it and know what to do with it,” she said.All of these experiences and questions transformed into the creation of CareCheck, Aima's proposed AI-powered breast-health platform. It will offer local-language guidance on breast self-awareness, allow users to record concerns, simplify medical information and locate nearby professional care. The platform is designed to guide women through breast self-checks, provide reminders and allow them to record changes and maintain a symptom history. Doctors and healthcare organisations are reviewing its content, wording and safety boundaries.“CareCheck does not diagnose cancer and it does not replace a doctor,” she said. Its purpose is more precise: helping a woman understand a concern, document it and reach appropriate care. She said that the platform is currently being finalised before becoming publicly available.After finishing school, she hoped to study computer science or computer engineering in US or UK, with a particular focus on artificial intelligence. “The emotional ties that I’ve had through cancer have made me realise that I can use CS within the healthcare industry without being a doctor or a nurse,” she said.
Article Summary: Saiyette Aima's grandmother was diagnosed with breast cancer when she was 10. The Dubai College student cut her locks and donated them through Locks of Hope, a Friends of Cancer Patients programme that provides wigs for people undergoing chemotherapy. Aima soon realised that a single campaign could only help so much. She then created Pink for Purpose, a cancer-awareness initiative.

Article Title: As the 9/11 attacks collapsed his office, a blind man's guide dog helped him down 78 flights to safety and saved his life
Article Text:
Roselle abruptly stopped at the top of a flight of stairs and led Hingson below ground, to shelter in a subway station.

September 11, 2026, will mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks which collapsed the World Trade Centre and led to the loss of thousands of lives. It also marks 25 years since Michael Hingson's life was saved by his guide dog, who helped him escape from the 78th story of the north tower of the centre.Hingson, blind since birth, had heard a muffled explosion as he stood in the doorway of his office. "We probably moved about 20 feet," he recalled to PEOPLE. Across the room, his colleague David Frank held onto a desk. “David and I actually said goodbye to each other,” said the 76-year-old, “because we thought we were going to take a 78-floor plunge to the street. Meanwhile, Roselle, Hingson's guide dog, a yellow Labrador retriever, was asleep beneath his desk.Hingson remembered that as the building was righting itself, Frank shouted, “Oh my God, Mike, there’s fire and smoke above us. We got to get out of here — right now.” A regional sales manager for a computer-storage company, Hingson and Frank had been preparing that morning to lead a seminar when a jet hijacked by al-Qaida struck the World Trade Centre at 8:46 am local time.Initially, though, the scale of the terror attack wasn’t clear.Hingson called his wife, Karen, at their home in Westfield, N.J., and told her there had been an emergency. Then he, Roselle and Frank, after a safe sweep of the office and knowing there were no other co-workers there, started retreating down to the ground. Just 15 floors above them, the tower was being consumed in the aftermath of the first plane crash.As the small group made the great escape, Roselle at times walked beside him, guiding him around obstacles. Other times, she walked behind him as he held the railing and climbed down. “The dogs don’t lead,” he explained. “They guide.”As they descended, Hingson repeatedly told Roselle: “Good dog, Roselle. You’re doing a great job.” “I knew she was going to sense the fear in everyone else, so I needed to let her know I was okay,” he said.Not just him, about 10 floors down, a woman behind them stopped and said, "I can't breathe, I can't go on." Hingson turned back to help, offering a hug while Roselle offered some comfort of her own, kisses. By the 50th floor, fear overtook Frank. “Mike, we’re going to die,” he yelled. “We’re not going to make it out of here.” But Hingson was determined.“Stop it, David,” he commanded. “If Roselle and I can go down these stairs, so can you.” The words calmed Frank, who started walking one floor ahead, telling Hingson what he saw as they went further.“Anyone within the sound of his voice heard someone who was calm, focused, going down the stairs and yelling to somebody else that he was okay,” Hingson said. “David had to be one of the major forces keeping people in that stairwell from panicking.”In time, firefighters began passing them on their way up, asking people to just "go down and get out" as they dealt with what was happening upstairs. In total, 343 New York City firefighters died that day when the World Trade Centre towers fell.As Hingson finally reached the lobby, an FBI agent directed him and Frank out of the complex. Soon, the 110-floor south tower was struck by another plane and began disintegrating. Hingson described it as a "rubble that was a combination of a freight train and a waterfall."“The first thing I thought was, ‘God, I can’t believe that you got us out of a building just to have it collapse on us,’” Hingson said. “And when I did that, I literally heard in my head a voice that said, ‘Don’t worry about what you can’t control. Focus on running with Roselle, and the rest will take care of itself.’ ”Out on the streets, Roselle abruptly stopped at the top of a flight of stairs and led Hingson below ground, to shelter in a subway station. When a police officer told them it was safe to leave, Hingson, Roselle and Frank, who had stayed with them, returned to the street and to the shocking sight of the south tower. Or where it should have stood.“David looked at us and said, ‘Oh my God, Mike, all I see are pillars of smoke hundreds of feet tall. It’s gone,’ ” Hingson shared. About 10 minutes later, the building where they had worked and where they had just escaped, the north tower, fell, too.Later that evening, Hingson finally returned home to New Jersey. Soon after the attacks, he moved to California and worked for Guide Dogs for the Blind. He found healing through talking to audiences about trust, teamwork and controlling fear.In 2002, Roselle received the Award for Canine Excellence (ACE) in the service dog category, and at the age of 14, died in June of 2011. Hingson now lives in Victorville, Calif., with Alamo, his ninth guide dog.
Article Summary: 2026 will mark 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks which collapsed the World Trade Centre and led to the loss of thousands of lives. It also marks 25 years since Michael Hingson's life was saved by his guide dog, who helped him escape from the 78th story of the north tower of the centre.

Article Title: Meet Linus Chen-Plotkin, the 18-year-old Philadelphia student who analysed more than 600 works by Mozart, Beethoven, Haydn, and Schubert and found Mozart's melodies were less predictable
Article Text:
Pic courtesy: Society for Science/Chris Ayers Photography

Teen proves Mozart’s music is unpredictable

Meet Linus Chen-Plotkin

Pic credit: Society for Science/Chris Ayers Photography

Beyond the project

Mozart’s versatility is unparalleled, even today. Ever wondered what made him the ultimate musical architect, with every phrase perfectly placed and every note seemingly inevitable? Well, an 18-year-old from Philadelphia may have found the answer! Linus Chen-Plotkin analysed more than 600 classical compositions and discovered something that musicologists have debated for centuries but never quite quantified. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s melodies are actually harder to predict than those of any other musician, including Beethoven and Schubert.For his Regeneron Science Talent Search project, Linus built three statistical tests to measure something he calls a melody's ‘memory’. His project, ‘Predictability and Statistical Memory in Classical Sonatas and Quartets’, was to find out how much earlier notes influence the ones that come after. The ‘memory’ tracks how much one note depends on the notes before it. High memory means earlier phrases keep influencing what comes next, making it more predictable. Low memory means the composer pivots quickly, keeping listeners slightly off-balance.The teenager ran these tests across 600-plus piano sonatas and string quartets by Joseph Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Ludwig van Beethoven, and Franz Schubert.What he found was striking. Mozart's music had shorter memory across all three tests, which means his melodies broke patterns faster. They were less predictable. Mozart honoured classical form while constantly slipping something unexpected past the listener's ear. In other words, perfection in Mozart's case didn't mean predictability; it meant something far harder to achieve.Linus’ findings finally provide an answer to understanding Mozart's works. For centuries, critics have thrown around words like ‘genius’ and ‘innovation’ without pinning down what they mean. Linus gave us a way to climb closer to the answer. The unpredictability is what made Mozart the genius he was. An 18-year-old wrestler from Philadelphia picked up statistical tools and told us something new about how Mozart's mind worked. Perhaps Mozart would have enjoyed that twist.Born to Joshua Plotkin and Alice Chen-Plotkin, Linus hails from Philadelphia, PA. He is a student at the Germantown Friends School. He's a varsity wrestler and an advanced Mandarin student. He is not a classical music prodigy who spent his childhood at conservatories, but he knows its mathematics. During the statistical analysis, he approached classical music as a dataset. He saw centuries of musical tradition as raw material for mathematical investigation. He believes his approach and other quantitative methods can help improve the understanding of areas that are typically studied qualitatively. Think music theory, art history, and literature. All these fields have relied on interpretation for centuries, but Linus thinks they don't have to stay that way. Music is not really alien to him. In fact, he also sings and plays blues guitar at The Twisted Tail bourbon bar during his spare time. While he isn’t neck-deep in work, he doubles as a radio operator. Linus is also a licensed amateur radio operator and a former member and soloist of the Philadelphia Boys Choir & Chorale. Few people his age have taken so many different angles on the same art form!Linus isn't stopping at the musical memory. He plans to go beyond. He's collaborating with a Johns Hopkins professor on analysing the grammatical rules of rhyme and metre in Geoffrey Chaucer's medieval poetry. He will be using the same approach on poems that belong to different centuries. The question is almost the same. Can we measure what makes great writing work? How does a poem resonate with the reader? What makes the best works the best?
Article Summary: Teen proves Mozart’s music is unpredictable. Linus Chen-Plotkin analysed more than 600 classical compositions. His project, ‘Predictability and Statistical Memory in Classical Sonatas and Quartets’ was to find out how much earlier notes influence the ones that come after. Mozart's music had shorter memory across all three tests, which means his melodies broke patterns faster.

Article Title: Another French heist: Thieves steal 4 paintings worth Rs 98 cr from Renoir museum; drop one while fleeing
Article Text:
File Photo: Visitors look at works by Auguste Renoir (Representative Image)

Two thieves broke into a museum dedicated to French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir in southern France on Tuesday and stole four artworks valued at around €9 million (approx Rs 98 crore), according to the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer.The suspects were spotted on the town’s surveillance cameras as they fled the Renoir Museum, with one of the stolen paintings dropped and recovered during their escape, mayor Bryan Masson said.The museum alarm went off at 5.48 am, and municipal police arrived five minutes later, Masson said.The Renoir Museum, opened in 1960 at the artist’s final home before his death in 1919, houses his paintings as well as personal belongings including his easel and wheelchair.The theft comes less than a year after eight items worth around $100 million were stolen from Paris’ Louvre in a daylight robbery.
Article Summary: Two thieves broke into a museum dedicated to French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir. They stole four artworks valued at around €9 million (approx Rs 98 crore) The suspects were spotted on the town’s surveillance cameras as they fled.

Article Title: In 2004, Toronto began using cold water from 83 metres beneath Lake Ontario to cool downtown buildings; today the system serves 200 buildings across 40 million sq ft
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

A 2004 cooling experiment

How lake water cools buildings

A network that keeps growing

Turning nature into infrastructure

Deep beneath the surface of Lake Ontario, a layer of naturally cold water has become an unlikely part of Toronto’s urban infrastructure. Instead of relying entirely on conventional air-conditioning systems to cool its downtown buildings, the Canadian city uses the lake’s cold temperature as a source of cooling energy. According to a report by the Daily Commercial News, water drawn from about 83 metres below the surface was being used as part of a district cooling network serving buildings in Toronto’s downtown core. What started more than two decades ago has since grown into one of North America’s largest district energy systems. Today, the network serves around 200 buildings and more than 40 million square feet of downtown real estate, including offices, hospitals, hotels, condominiums, educational institutions and data centres.Toronto-based Enwave had begun using its Deep Lake Water Cooling (DLWC) system to cool buildings in the downtown core. The report explained that the system drew water from a permanently cold layer about 83 metres beneath Lake Ontario and described it as the largest renewable lake-source cooling system of its kind at the time. The project initially produced enough air conditioning to cool about 20 million square feet of office space.It was also reported to reduce electricity use by 75% compared with traditional air conditioning and was expected to eliminate about 40,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.The key idea behind the system is that the water at the bottom of the lake remains cold enough to provide useful cooling even during Toronto’s hot summers. Rather than using the lake water directly inside buildings, Enwave uses its low temperature to transfer cooling energy into a separate water network.The process begins deep in Lake Ontario, where cold water is drawn through intake pipes and sent to the Island Filtration Plant. The water is treated before reaching the John Street Pumping Station, where heat exchangers transfer its cooling energy to Enwave’s separate chilled-water system. This distinction is important: the lake water itself does not circulate through the buildings' air-conditioning systems. Instead, its cold temperature is used to cool another water loop. Heat exchangers transfer the cooling energy, creating chilled water that can then be distributed through underground pipes to connected buildings.Once inside a building, the chilled water absorbs heat from the building’s cooling system. The warmed water returns to the district system, where it can be cooled again and circulated back through the network. This centralised approach means individual buildings do not necessarily need to operate large conventional chiller plants of their own. Enwave says the system provides an alternative to traditional cooling towers and equipment, which can represent significant capital and operating costs for large buildings.The system has expanded considerably since its launch. Enwave’s current information for Toronto states that its district energy network serves 200 buildings and more than 40 million square feet of downtown real estate. The network is supported by four interconnected downtown plants and about 25 miles (40 kilometres) of underground pipes. Its customers include hospitals, commercial offices, hotels, condominiums, institutions and data centres. The Deep Lake Water Cooling system remains the main anchor of the wider district-energy network. Some individual buildings have also benefited by no longer needing conventional cooling infrastructure. According to Enwave, Brookfield Place, which contains more than 2.6 million square feet of office space, eliminated the need for conventional chiller plants after connecting to the system.Toronto’s system demonstrates how a natural feature can become part of a city’s energy infrastructure. The cold water deep beneath Lake Ontario provides a stable source of cooling energy, while a centralised network distributes that cooling to hundreds of buildings. The system can reduce peak electricity-system generation compared with the demand that would otherwise be required by traditional cooling methods. That makes the concept particularly relevant for dense cities, where large numbers of buildings can place significant pressure on electricity systems during hot weather.More than 20 years after the original project began, Toronto’s Deep Lake Water Cooling system shows how district energy can move beyond individual building-by-building solutions. By using the naturally cold conditions deep within Lake Ontario and combining them with underground infrastructure and heat-exchange technology, the city has turned cold lake water into a large-scale cooling resource for its urban core.
Article Summary: Toronto-based Enwave has been using lake water to cool buildings in the city's downtown core since 2004. The project initially produced enough air conditioning to cool about 20 million square feet of office space. It was also reported to reduce electricity use by 75% compared with traditional air conditioning and was expected to eliminate about 40,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions. Today, the network serves around 200 buildings and more than 40 million sq ft of downtown real estate.

Article Title: Mississippi teen Madalyn Sullivan wrote an autism-acceptance book inspired by her sister and sent it to libraries in all 82 counties; she has now finished second at Miss America’s Teen
Article Text:
As Miss Mississippi’s Teen, Sullivan planned to use her platform to support families affected by autism.

A mission inspired by her sister

Reading the book with her sister

Madalyn Sullivan, Miss Mississippi’s Teen and an Oxford native, has finished as first runner-up at Miss America’s Teen. The high school student reached the national stage after years of advocating for autism acceptance, inspired by her sister, and using that experience to create Millie’s Mission.Sullivan competed through a week of events before the final competition. According to Super Talk FM's report, her schedule included interviews, a talent portion, preliminary competitions and public appearances. The final was held at the Kravis Center for the Performing Arts, where Miss Utah’s Teen Elle Anderson was crowned Miss America’s Teen 2027.Sullivan finished second among the five finalists. Anderson took the title, followed by Sullivan, Miss South Carolina’s Teen Logan Wells, Miss Texas’ Teen Zoe Zogleman and Miss Minnesota’s Teen Natalia Yurecko.Sullivan received a $9,000 scholarship for finishing as first runner-up. Earlier in the week, she won the Evening Wear Preliminary competition, earning another $1,500 scholarship.For Sullivan, however, the pageant is only one part of the work she has been doing. Away from the stage, the Oxford High School student has been using her own family experience to promote autism acceptance through an initiative called Millie’s Mission.Sullivan’s interest in autism advocacy began with her younger sister. She said her sister was diagnosed with autism when she was 2, while Sullivan was 5 years old.“My sister was diagnosed with autism when she was 2, and I was 5 at the time, and since then I have tried to be one of her biggest advocates,” Sullivan said, as quoted by WAPT.Sullivan said she grew up reading to her sister’s classroom about autism. That experience eventually led her to create something of her own that could be shared with children and families.She co-authored a children’s book called “Meet Millie”. The book was created as part of Millie’s Mission, the initiative she founded to promote autism acceptance and encourage a more inclusive society for people with autism.Sullivan eventually took the book across Mississippi. She said “Meet Millie” is available on Amazon and that she donated copies to public libraries in all 82 counties in the state.The project has also given Sullivan a way to work alongside the sister who inspired it. Sullivan said her sister joins her when she reads “Meet Millie” and that the two have fun during those sessions.For Sullivan, the book is connected directly to the larger purpose of Millie’s Mission. “The goal of Millie's Mission is to create a more inclusive society for those with autism,” she said.As Miss Mississippi’s Teen, Sullivan had planned to use her year-long platform to encourage communities to support families affected by autism.Sullivan is also active outside her advocacy and pageant work. She is an Oxford High School student and takes part in several school activities. She is a member of the dance team, runs cross country, sings in the choir and participates in the theatre programme.
Article Summary: Madalyn Sullivan, Miss Mississippi’s Teen, has finished as first runner-up at Miss America's Teen 2027. The Oxford High School student has been using her own family experience to promote autism acceptance through an initiative called Millie's Mission. She co-authored a children's book called ‘Meet Millie’ as part of the initiative.

Article Title: In Japan, local authorities have installed signs warning drivers that cats may suddenly dash into the road, using playful illustrations to make the danger memorable
Article Text:
Japan installs playful signs to warn drivers about cats

The playful designs are based on a real danger for cats

Tsushima uses warning signs to protect an endangered wild cat

Japan combines warning signs with other wildlife protection measures

A simple warning becomes a memorable road-safety message

An unusual road-safety idea in Japan is turning an everyday danger into something drivers are unlikely to forget. In parts of the country, signs featuring cats warn motorists that an animal could suddenly run into the road. Some of the designs are deliberately playful, using striking cat illustrations rather than conventional wildlife-warning imagery. The idea is rooted in a genuine road-safety concern. Cats can suddenly enter roads while chasing birds or insects, and their sensitivity to noise and light can sometimes cause them to freeze when confronted by a vehicle. Organisations and local authorities have therefore used visual warnings to encourage motorists to slow down and stay alert. The approach has also been adapted for wildlife conservation, including efforts to protect Japan's endangered Tsushima leopard cat from road traffic.One of the most distinctive examples came from Yellow Hat, a Japanese automotive retailer that launched a road-safety campaign focused specifically on reducing cat traffic accidents. As part of the campaign, the company created a cat warning sign designed to catch drivers' attention and remind them that cats can suddenly enter the road.The design was developed with supervision from a Kyoto University animal psychology research team specialising in companion-animal behaviour. Rather than relying on a standard warning image, the sign attempted to recreate the expression and posture of a cat about to dash into the road. Yellow Hat said the aim was to create a warning that would be particularly effective at attracting attention. The campaign was launched around Cat Day in February 2022, with a sign installed near a school in Tokyo's Shibuya area.Behind the amusing appearance of these signs is a serious problem. Yellow Hat explained that cats can run into roads because of their natural hunting behaviour, particularly when they chase birds or insects. The company also highlighted another difficulty. Cats are highly sensitive to sounds and light, and when confronted by a vehicle they can sometimes become unable to move instead of escaping from the road. That combination can create dangerous situations for both animals and motorists. The campaign therefore encouraged drivers to pay attention to cats while driving and to approach areas where animals may be present with greater care. The unusual artwork was intended to make the warning stand out rather than disappear among the many conventional signs motorists encounter on roads.The same basic idea becomes even more important on Tsushima, an island in southwestern Japan that is home to the critically endangered Tsushima leopard cat. Japan's Environment Ministry has repeatedly used warning signs and other measures to reduce vehicle collisions involving the species. The Tsushima Wildlife Conservation Center has installed warning boards near areas where leopard cats are known to occur or where previous accidents have happened. In one documented effort, authorities and local partners installed signs around an area with a history of leopard-cat traffic accidents, including signs designed to reflect vehicle headlights at night. Drivers are encouraged to slow down and remain alert, particularly because the animals are active around roads and can suddenly appear in the path of vehicles.The signs are only one part of a broader strategy. On Tsushima, conservation authorities have also used speed warnings, road markings, fencing, under-road passages and other measures intended to reduce the likelihood of animals entering traffic. The Environment Ministry says road accidents remain one of the most serious threats facing the Tsushima leopard cat, whose population is estimated at around 100 individuals. Historical records have documented numerous traffic-related deaths, while officials continue to run awareness campaigns and monitor accident hotspots. In 2024, the Environment Ministry also conducted a road-safety campaign after a leopard cat was killed during the daytime, highlighting that drivers should not assume the animals are only a nighttime concern.What makes Japan's cat-warning signs particularly striking is the way they combine a serious safety message with an approachable visual style. Instead of presenting wildlife as an abstract road hazard, the signs put the animal itself at the centre of the warning. That can make drivers more likely to notice and remember the message, especially when the artwork is unusual enough to stand out from conventional road signage. But the signs should not be mistaken for evidence of a single nationwide programme requiring cat-warning signs on Japanese roads. They represent different local and organisational efforts, ranging from campaigns aimed at ordinary domestic cats to conservation measures protecting endangered wild cats. Together, they show how a simple roadside warning can be made more memorable while addressing a very real problem.
Article Summary: Japan installs warning signs featuring cats to warn drivers about cats. The playful designs are based on a real danger for cats. Cats can suddenly enter roads while chasing birds or insects. Their sensitivity to noise and light can sometimes cause them to freeze when confronted by a vehicle.

Article Title: Soon, Aussies could opt out of social media algorithms
Article Text:
Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms.

Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister said Monday. The draft law requiring a “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week.It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.“A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility they get out of it,” communications minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC. “A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm -- but we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place, and they should respect that choice.”“We should give Australians more choice over what they should see on their feeds,” she said.Social media firms have long faced scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to sensational or extreme content to keep them scrolling. Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in Dec, part of a world-first crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and “predatory algorithms”.The UK, France and others have followed suit. Data last month found that under-16s in Australia were increasing their use of social m­e­dia apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.
Article Summary: A draft law requiring a “digital duty of care’ is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week. It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste. Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in Dec.

Article Title: In the 1980s, Rutgers researcher Thomas Nosker mixed milk jugs with discarded Big Mac containers to make structural plastic lumber; about 1.5 million US rail ties have kept an estimated 300 million po
Article Text:
US rail ties have kept pounds of plastic out of landfills. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

HDPE milk bottles were too cheap to recycle

Combining HDPE with polystyrene from Big Mac containers

Proving plastic could replace wood

Glass milk bottles. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

1.5 million railway ties across the United States

Where the technology is used today

During the 1980s, Thomas Nosker was a doctoral student at Rutgers University who set out to address a mounting problem. It was the rapid accumulation of plastic packaging waste with no practical recycling pathway, according to a Rutgers Research profile of his work. Packaging materials such as plastic were rapidly replacing glass containers on store shelves, and the used bottles were piling up with no practical way to recycle them, so most of it was simply headed for landfills. This material was what Nosker eventually came up with after countless experiments and it is now called structural plastic lumber, a material that can replace wood and steel in their structural forms. Years later, that same material was used to manufacture roughly 1.5 million railroad ties across the United States, keeping an estimated 300 million pounds of plastic out of landfills, waterways and oceans.Bottles manufactured using polyethylene terephthalate, called PET, could easily be sorted and processed for resale into items such as carpet or insulated clothing. High-density polyethylene, called HDPE, which is the plastic in milk jugs, was more problematic. As Nosker notes, the price of HDPE was so low that it didn't make economic sense to wash used milk jugs before recycling them on their own.It was during this time that the real breakthrough came, as Nosker began experimenting with blends rather than treating each plastic separately.He mixed HDPE with polystyrene salvaged from discarded Big Mac containers, the clamshell packaging McDonald's had used for its sandwiches before phasing it out beginning in the late 1980s and continuing into the early 1990s amid environmental pressure. Blending the two plastics sidestepped the economic problem entirely, since the finished composite drew its value from strength rather than the purity of either input material, meaning the low-value HDPE no longer needed to be washed or sorted on its own to be useful. Nosker found that certain blend ratios produced a much stronger material, likely because the particles of each plastic interlocked rather than separating.Convincing an industry built entirely around wood lumber to accept a plastic substitute was never going to be easy; the material needed to prove its durability in the field, not just in a lab. As described in Rutgers's account of the invention, Nosker and his colleagues took a show-don't-tell approach, building actual structures rather than relying only on laboratory data, because wood had long been the default building material and skepticism toward a plastic alternative ran deep.In 2002, Nosker helped build New Jersey's first structural recycled-plastic bridge, a 40 to 42-foot vehicular span over the Mullica River in Wharton State Forest near Atsion Lake, in the Pine Barrens, an ecologically sensitive region where wood and steel structures typically degrade faster due to moisture and acidity in the soil. The accomplishment may have helped the material gain wider acceptance in the U.S. Army; in 2009, the Army demonstrated that a bridge built with the technology could carry a 73-ton M1 Abrams tank at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.Among other qualities of the final product, one should consider its density. As stated in Rutgers Research, the material is now used worldwide in bridges, railway ties, docks, and picnic tables, and has so far gone into roughly 1.5 million railway ties in the US. With each tie weighing approximately 200 pounds, Rutgers estimates that some 300 million pounds of plastic have been kept out of landfills and oceans as a result.Rutgers has since licensed the technology to two firms, AXION International Inc. of Zanesville, Ohio, and Sicut Enterprises Limited, based in London. According to Rutgers, both companies manufacture railroad ties and building materials from the recycled composite. In addition to railway ties, plastic lumber has found use on docks, picnic benches, park benches and parking bollards all over the U.S. and internationally. The Chicago Transit Authority has used the ties on its elevated tracks for track repair in an urban setting.Nosker holds more than 82 U.S. patents and pending patent applications related to plastic lumber and its manufacturing processes, according to Rutgers, work that has generated substantial licensing revenue for the university over the decades. He is currently working on the development of plastic composites reinforced by graphene for making light yet strong materials for use in vehicles and military applications. Even so, the plastic lumber project remains among Nosker's most visible contributions, a solution to a packaging waste problem that began with two of the most common items in American refrigerators and fast-food bags: a plastic milk jug and a foam sandwich box.
Article Summary: Thomas Nosker, a doctoral student at Rutgers University, developed structural plastic lumber in the 1980s. The material is now used worldwide in bridges, railway ties, docks, and picnic tables, and has so far gone into roughly 1.5 million railway ties in the US. With each tie weighing approximately 200 pounds, Rutgers estimates that some 300 million pounds of plastic have been kept out of landfills.

Article Title: In 2007, Wisconsin used dye to trace why 229 people got sick; septic-tank wastewater reached the drinking well in 6 days, while infiltration-field dye took 15
Article Text:
Door County, Wisconsin used dye to trace why 229 people got sick. Image credits: Wikipedia

The outbreak: 229 cases, one contaminated well

The red dye test revelations

Why the Wisconsin Bedrock made this possible

A wider problem across northeastern Wisconsin

Quantitative Microbial Risk Assessment for Contaminated Private Wells in the Fractured Dolomite Aquifer of Kewaunee County, Wisconsin

2 chamber septic tank under construction. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

What the findings changed

In June 2007, a brand-new restaurant in Door County, Wisconsin, provided the setting for perhaps the most extensively documented outbreak of waterborne disease of recent times in the USA, according to the CDC's Surveillance for Waterborne Disease Outbreaks Associated with Drinking Water, United States, 2007–2008, the MMWR summary covering 2007-2008 outbreaks. According to the same CDC report, 229 cases of acute gastroenteritis occurred among customers and staff at the restaurant not long after it opened, and six people were hospitalized. All this to address the single question of how human waste found its way into a well that complied with all the state building codes.First, a case-control study by Borchardt and colleagues ruled out food poisoning and found that drinking the restaurant's well water was associated with illness (odds ratio = 3.2, a measure of how much more likely illness was in one group versus another). Second, testing detected norovirus genogroup I, a group of viral strains that cause acute gastroenteritis, in the restaurant's well water at around 50 genomic copies per liter. Third, genetic sequencing confirmed the same viral strain, genotype GI.2, in the patients' stool samples, the restaurant's septic tank, and the well water. Together, these findings identify the well as the primary source of infection in the outbreak, as documented by Borchardt and colleagues in the journal Ground Water.The well is 85 meters deep, and the septic system sits 188 meters away, separated from it by a 35-meter-thick soil layer called the vadose zone (the unsaturated ground above the water table).In order to determine how the contamination got to the well, two different dyes were injected into two parts of the septic system, the tanks and the infiltration field. Borchardt and colleagues reported that dye injected into the septic tanks reached the well within six days through a leaking fitting, while dye released into the infiltration field took about fifteen days to arrive. This is where the account of wastewater reaching the drinking water well in about a week began. Wastewater from both the tanks and the infiltration field ultimately reached the restaurant's well. This meant the septic effluent was carried by groundwater directly into the drinking water well.Door County is located on top of a fractured dolomite aquifer of Silurian age. This rock formation is made up of joints and bedding-plane channels that let water, along with whatever pollutants it carries, move rapidly with little natural filtration. As noted earlier, both the well and the septic system were built entirely in accordance with the state codes in place at the time. Adherence to those codes turned out not to be enough for this particular geology: the setback distances assumed groundwater would move slowly enough to be filtered naturally over weeks or months, but the dye tests showed it could travel through the fractured dolomite in a matter of days.This is not an isolated case. A related 2021 study by Burch and colleagues,, examined the same aquifer system in a nearby county, where roughly half the county's population, an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 people, relies on private wells. Using a year-long, countywide pathogen occurrence data set as the input to their quantitative microbial risk model, Burch and colleagues estimated, rather than directly observed, that contaminated private wells could be responsible for as many as 301 modeled cases of acute gastrointestinal illness per year in the county.Of the 301 modeled cases, the study attributed about 230 a year to cattle manure and 12 to human sources. The same study found that Cryptosporidium parvum alone accounted for an estimated 190 of those cases each year, the largest share among the eight pathogens modeled. This pathogen-level figure overlaps with, rather than adds to, the source-level breakdown above (230 bovine, 12 human), since the same modeled illnesses can be counted twice: once by fecal source and once by pathogen. Microbial source tracking allowed the researchers to distinguish bovine from human contamination, an important capability given that the Kewaunee County dolomite aquifer underlies many dairy farms and septic systems.Together, the two cases have reshaped how experts think about the risks of groundwater contamination in fractured bedrock areas. Inspection of the water supply or proper septic-system design does not eliminate risk. The CDC's national waterborne disease outbreak surveillance report covered the Door County case directly, noting that pathogens reached the water through cracks in the dolomite that created a hydraulic connection between the septic system and the well. The same CDC report found that, among the 36 outbreaks linked to drinking water in 2007 and 2008, 13 of the 21 outbreaks tied to source-water, treatment, or distribution deficiencies were caused by untreated groundwater. The report also noted that EPA regulations do not apply to private wells, and that more than half of the drinking-water outbreaks it reviewed were linked to untreated or inadequately treated groundwater.
Article Summary: In 2007, a restaurant in Door County, Wisconsin, provided the setting for perhaps the most extensively documented outbreak of waterborne disease of recent times in the USA. The well is 85 meters deep, and the septic system sits 188 meters away, separated from it by a 35-meter-thick soil layer called the vadose zone. Wastewater from the tanks and the infiltration field ultimately reached the restaurant's well.

Article Title: Meet Celine Zhang, the 18-year-old New Jersey student who developed a way to prove a digital puzzle was solved without revealing the answer
Article Text:
Zhang also serves as an instructor and teaching assistant at AlphaStar Academy where he teaches computer science classes and helps students with their questions.

From games to cyber security

A student with many interests

Beyond the project

Think of a situation where you are working on a challenging puzzle when someone asks you to demonstrate that you’ve solved it, but you can’t show them your work. That sounds like near impossibility. But for 18-year-old Celine Zhang of Princeton, New Jersey, that challenge became the foundation for an innovative computer science project: building a better robot. According to a report by Society for Science, Zhang’s computer science project at the Regeneron Science Talent Search was based on a mathematical idea called zero-knowledge proofs. These are techniques that allow a person to prove to someone else that they know something without revealing the knowledge, mentions the report. Zhang realized the idea in puzzle games with a moving avatar that fuses blocks. Her method allows a player who has solved a puzzle to prove that they know the solution without just giving it away to another player. Instead of giving away the entire answer, the solver might offer some particular, but limited, guidance that lets others check off the achievement. The idea is that it gives you the ability to build trust without giving away the solution .Though the project is based on puzzles, Zhang’s work has applications far beyond games. The same principles that underlie her approach could potentially be useful in fields like digital security, machine learning, and blockchain authentication, where it can be valuable to prove that someone has the right information without revealing sensitive data. Her project demonstrates how an abstract mathematical concept can be tied to real-world problems in technology, transforming an ordinary question about puzzles into an investigation of privacy and authentication.Zhang is a student at Phillips Exeter Academy and is co-head of the engineering club and co-leader of the Junior Computer Programming Club. Through the programming club, she teaches beginning computer science to elementary and middle school students in the Exeter area. Her interests extend beyond the realm of technology. Zhang is the section leader for the sopranos in PEADQUACS, a co-ed a cappella group that performs at school showcases, admissions events and community gatherings.Zhang also serves as an instructor and teaching assistant at AlphaStar Academy where he teaches computer science classes and helps students with their questions. She enjoys being game-ready when she’s not working on computer science or music. Fun fact about her? Zhang always has a deck of cards with her, in case she can play the strategy game Avalon with a friend.Images Courtesy: Society for Science and istock
Article Summary: Celine Zhang, 18, of Princeton, New Jersey, is a student at Phillips Exeter Academy. Her computer science project at the Regeneron Science Talent Search was based on a mathematical idea called zero-knowledge proofs. Zhang realized the idea in puzzle games with a moving avatar that fuses blocks.

Article Title: Lightning struck an 1890 Georgia mansion; its owners drove away unaware the turret was burning until passersby spotted flames, and firefighters kept the main floor undamaged
Article Text:
Owners did not know the mansion had caught fire

Fire contained to the turret

A historic Carrollton landmark

Repairs planned as business continues

A lightning strike set fire to the turret of a historic Georgia mansion Saturday night, damaging its distinctive steeple and balcony but leaving the business operating inside largely untouched, according to FOX 5 Atlanta, which reported the incident on September 6. The fire broke out at the Maple Street Mansion at 401 Maple Street in Carrollton after lightning struck the building during a severe storm. The mansion, which dates to 1890, currently houses The Heirloom Store, a retail business run by owners Rhett and Malina. The Heirloom Store’s own account of the property confirms the mansion was built in 1890 and has served as a landmark in Carrollton for more than a century.The incident unfolded as the owners waited out the storm nearby. According to the account shared by the owners and reported by FOX 5 Atlanta, Rhett and Malina had been parked outside as the weather worsened when a powerful lightning bolt struck. They did not initially realize that the historic building had been hit.They briefly went inside after noticing flickering lights, resetting a breaker before leaving the property. By then, however, the lightning strike had ignited the upper portion of the mansion.It was passersby who noticed flames coming from the roof and called 911, bringing emergency crews to the property before the fire could spread further.Firefighters were able to confine the blaze to the mansion’s upper exterior. The turret and steeple sustained significant structural damage, as did the balcony. But the fire did not make its way down into the main floor, where The Heirloom Store operates.The owners said the store’s merchandise and main-floor interior escaped both fire and water damage. That distinction is particularly significant for the historic property, which has been used for commercial purposes for decades. The Heirloom Store describes the building as a roughly 33,000-square-foot landmark with a history stretching back to its construction by L.C. Mandeville in the late 19th century. The property has housed restaurants, event spaces and other businesses over the years.The Maple Street Mansion is more than a commercial property in Carrollton. The Victorian-era building is closely tied to the city’s history and was originally the home of L.C. Mandeville, an influential businessman associated with Mandeville Mills. Historical records held by the University of West Georgia identify the property at 401 Maple Street as the L.C. Mandeville House and document its significance to Carrollton’s development.The building also survived a potential demolition in 2014, according to The Heirloom Store’s history of the property, before entering another chapter as a retail and community space.While the visible damage is concentrated high above the main floor, the full extent of the lightning strike’s impact has not yet been established. A detailed inspection was expected once crews could safely examine the structure in daylight, particularly for electrical damage that may not be immediately visible.For now, the owners intend to begin exterior repairs while keeping The Heirloom Store open. What began with a lightning strike could therefore have ended very differently. Instead, a blaze high in the mansion’s iconic turret was spotted in time, firefighters stopped it from descending into the building, and the business below was left standing.
Article Summary: A lightning strike set fire to the turret of a historic Georgia mansion Saturday night, damaging its distinctive steeple and balcony. The fire broke out at the Maple Street Mansion at 401 Maple Street in Carrollton after lightning struck the building during a severe storm. The mansion, which dates to 1890, currently houses The Heirloom Store, a retail business run by owners Rhett and Malina. The owners did not initially realize that the historic building had been hit.

Article Title: Michael Bloomberg was fired from a Wall Street bank after 15 years. He used his $10 million payout to build a $109 billion fortune and has given away $25.4 billion
Article Text:
Michael Bloomberg was fired after 15 years at Salomon Brothers

Bloomberg used his $10 million payout to start a company

The Bloomberg Terminal became the company's breakthrough

Bloomberg expanded into news and media

Bloomberg's fortune reached more than $109 billion

Bloomberg has given away $25.4 billion

Johns Hopkins received billions in Bloomberg donations

His philanthropy extends beyond education

A Wall Street setback became the beginning of a new fortune

Michael Bloomberg was 39 when his 15-year career at Wall Street investment bank Salomon Brothers came to an end in 1981. A general partner at the firm, Bloomberg left as Salomon was being acquired by Phibro Corporation and received about $10 million for his stake. Rather than use the money to retire or join another Wall Street firm, he put it towards an idea shaped by his years in finance. Bloomberg believed financial professionals needed faster and more efficient access to market information, and he set out to build a company around that idea. The venture became Bloomberg LP and eventually grew into a global financial information and media company. Forbes now estimates Bloomberg's fortune at about $109.4 billion and his lifetime charitable giving at $25.4 billion.Bloomberg joined Salomon Brothers in 1966 after graduating from Johns Hopkins University and Harvard Business School. He began in an entry-level position and worked his way up through the investment bank, eventually becoming a general partner. He also took responsibility for the firm's information systems, giving him an early understanding of how technology could change the way financial professionals accessed and processed market data.In 1981, Salomon Brothers was acquired by Phibro Corporation, and Bloomberg was among the partners who left the firm. Bloomberg has described the event as being fired from the only full-time job he had known. His departure ended a 15-year Wall Street career, but it also gave him the financial resources and independence to pursue his own business idea.When Bloomberg left Salomon Brothers, he received roughly $10 million for his partnership stake. The money became the financial foundation for his next venture. Instead of looking for another position in finance, he founded Innovative Market Systems in 1981 with former Salomon colleagues Thomas Secunda, Duncan MacMillan and Charles Zegar. The company's objective was to provide financial professionals with better access to market information through technology. Bloomberg had seen at Salomon how valuable timely financial data could be, as well as how difficult it could be to gather information from multiple sources. His new company aimed to put data, analytics and financial information directly in front of users through computer terminals.The company secured an important early customer when Merrill Lynch agreed to purchase Bloomberg's financial information terminals. Merrill Lynch eventually ordered 20 terminals and invested $30 million in the company for a 30% stake. The system developed into the Bloomberg Terminal, which combined real-time financial data, analytics, news and communications in a single platform. The terminal gave traders and other financial professionals a faster way to access information and analyse markets. As more financial institutions adopted the technology, Bloomberg LP grew from a small start-up into a major financial information business. The terminal remains one of the company's best-known products and became the foundation for Bloomberg's expansion into other areas.Bloomberg's business eventually moved beyond financial terminals. The company launched Bloomberg Business News in 1990, later known as Bloomberg News, creating a newsroom focused heavily on financial and business reporting. Bloomberg LP subsequently expanded into television, radio, magazines and digital media. The combination of financial data, technology and journalism became a defining feature of the company. Bloomberg's business model also allowed the company to build a large recurring-revenue operation serving financial institutions around the world. Over time, Bloomberg LP became a global financial information and media company, while Bloomberg retained a substantial ownership stake.Bloomberg's wealth is closely tied to his ownership of Bloomberg LP. Forbes estimates that he owns about 88% of the privately held company. Forbes' current real-time estimate puts his net worth at approximately $109.4 billion, although the figure can change as valuations and other financial factors change. His fortune therefore represents the estimated value of his assets and business interests rather than $109 billion held as cash. The Bloomberg Terminal and the company's broader financial information operations have been central to creating and sustaining that wealth over the decades since he left Salomon Brothers.Bloomberg has also become one of America's largest individual philanthropists. Through Bloomberg Philanthropies and other charitable giving, he has directed billions of dollars towards public health, education, climate and environmental initiatives, arts and culture, and efforts to improve cities and government. Forbes estimates that Bloomberg's lifetime charitable giving reached $25.4 billion by the end of 2025. The figure includes billions committed to organisations and initiatives across several fields, making philanthropy a major part of how Bloomberg has used his wealth.Education has been one of the largest beneficiaries of Bloomberg's philanthropy. In 2018, Bloomberg announced a $1.8 billion gift to Johns Hopkins University, his alma mater, to support financial aid and help the university maintain need-blind admissions. He later pledged another $1 billion to the university in 2024 to support financial aid for medical students. His total giving to Johns Hopkins has consequently reached more than $3.5 billion, according to Forbes. Bloomberg has also committed hundreds of millions of dollars to strengthen historically Black medical schools and support other educational initiatives.Bloomberg's charitable work covers a broad range of issues. Bloomberg Philanthropies supports programmes focused on reducing tobacco use, improving public health, tackling climate change, strengthening cities and local governments, expanding educational opportunities and supporting arts organisations. His climate giving has included major commitments to the transition away from coal and efforts to accelerate clean energy. He has also supported initiatives addressing gun violence and other public-health challenges. Bloomberg's approach has often involved combining large financial commitments with long-term programmes designed to influence policy and institutions.Bloomberg's journey from Salomon Brothers to one of the world's richest people began with an unexpected career setback. At 39, after 15 years on Wall Street, he left the firm with about $10 million and chose to build a financial technology company rather than return to another investment bank. The idea eventually became Bloomberg LP, transforming how financial professionals accessed market information and creating the foundation of his fortune. More than four decades later, Forbes estimates that Bloomberg is worth about $109.4 billion and has given away $25.4 billion during his lifetime. What began as the end of a Wall Street career ultimately became the starting point for one of the world's largest financial information businesses and one of America's biggest philanthropic fortunes.
Article Summary: Michael Bloomberg was fired after 15 years at Salomon Brothers in 1981. He received about $10 million for his stake in the Wall Street investment bank. Instead of looking for another job, he founded Innovative Market Systems. The company's objective was to provide financial professionals with better access to market information through technology. The Bloomberg Terminal became the company's breakthrough product. Bloomberg's wealth is closely tied to his ownership of Bloomberg LP. Forbes estimates that he owns about 88% of the privately held company.

Article Title: Meet Suborno Isaac Bari: The maths prodigy who caught Barack Obama’s attention, skipped five grades and graduated high school at 12
Article Text:
PC: Instagram

Suborno Bari’s early maths skills surprised his parents

Bari's academic path soon moved beyond the usual timetable

University classes became part of his high school years

At seven, Bari was already speaking at Indian universities

PC: Instagram

He entered NYU with plans to finish college by 14

Teaching remained part of the plan

His interests extended beyond Maths and Physics

At 2 years old, Suborno Isaac Bari was already doing something that would later become a defining detail of his childhood: reciting the periodic table. Mathematics was developing alongside that early fascination with science, and his parents soon realised that ordinary lessons were not quite enough to contain his curiosity. Years later, the New York student would take an accelerated route through school, skipping several grades before graduating from Malverne High School at just 12 in June 2024. By then, he had already experienced university-level classes and had been invited to lecture at colleges in India. His next step was New York University, where he planned to study mathematics and physics.Bari had also set himself an unusually early academic target, hoping to complete his undergraduate degree by spring 2026 and eventually pursue doctoral research in mathematics.The first signs did not come from a classroom or a competition. They appeared during ordinary lessons at home.Bari's mother, Shaheda, was teaching him basic arithmetic when he was around two. His father, Rashidul Bari, later recalled that his son's answers soon became less interesting than the questions that followed them. A simple addition problem could turn into a question about whether the same principle worked with unknown numbers.His father was studying mathematics at the time and initially did not regard the behaviour as particularly extraordinary. That changed when the questioning continued across different mathematical ideas.He eventually described what he was seeing to one of his professors. The professor urged him to pay closer attention to the child's abilities.Around the same period, Bari was also becoming fascinated by science. His family says he was able to recite the elements of the periodic table at the age of two, an accomplishment that later became one of the most frequently reported details of his childhood.Bari's education was gradually reorganised around his academic ability. Instead of moving through each school year in sequence, he skipped several grades.He told Good Morning America, that by the time he graduated from Malverne High School, he had bypassed 5th, 6th, 7th, 9th and 11th grades. He completed his fourth, eighth, 10th and 12th grades within the district while also passing the New York State Regents examinations needed for graduation.That made him 12 years old at graduation. The school did not simply place him in classes with much older pupils and leave him there. Rebecca Gottesman, the district's director of K-12 counselling, said staff and the family worked on an arrangement that allowed Bari to take more advanced academic courses while retaining opportunities to interact with children closer to his own age.For part of that arrangement, he attended higher-level classes and then returned to younger pupils for electives and other activities. The aim was to keep his academic work moving quickly without ignoring the social side of growing up.The numbers attached to his school record were striking even without his age being taken into account. Reportedly, he scored 1,500 on the SAT and 34 on the ACT, while also completing five Advanced Placement classes.Before graduating, Bari had taken non-degree courses at several universities in the New York area, including NYU, Stony Brook University, the City University of New York and Brooklyn College. The experience introduced him to longer classes, heavier workloads and material that was compressed into a much shorter period than he was used to at school.Bari's academic activities had also taken him outside the United States.When he was seven, he began receiving invitations from universities in India to give lectures. He has spoken about mathematics and physics to university audiences, including at Mumbai University.Those appearances gave him contact with students, lecturers and university administrators well before he became a university student himself. His father said the experience exposed Bari to people working at different levels of higher education.The family has also said that former US president Barack Obama sent Bari a letter in 2016 recognising his work and accomplishments.Bari was accepted by New York University with a scholarship to study Mathematics and Physics. He described him as the youngest student in the university's 193 years, based on the information available at the time.His plans were ambitious. Suborno told CNN, “I hope to graduate college at 14 in spring 2026”. He added, “If I ever decide to do a second Ph.D., it will be in physics, but mainly I want to focus on math.”There was a familiar thread running through Bari's plans for the future: teaching.Both of his parents work in education. His father teaches physics at Brooklyn Technical High School, while his mother is an elementary school teacher. Bari has said that he would eventually like to become a professor of mathematics and physics.The ambition is not simply about holding an academic title. He has spoken about wanting to make mathematics and science easier for other people to understand, particularly those who may not have access to the same educational opportunities.That interest had appeared early in his life. Giving lectures to university students in India as a child meant that teaching was already something he had experienced before reaching university himself.Mathematics and Physics dominate Bari's academic story, but his family has described interests outside those subjects too.He has been involved in debate and painting and plays the piano. His time at Malverne was also not entirely separated from ordinary school life. The district made an effort to keep him connected with students his own age even as his academic work moved ahead.That balance became part of the school's approach to his education. Gottesman said the district considered his social and emotional development alongside his academic ability.
Article Summary: Suborno Isaac Bari was able to recite the elements of the periodic table at the age of two. By the time he was 12, he had already been invited to give lectures in India. He was accepted by New York University with plans to finish college by 14.

Article Title: In 1895, lightning ignited a massive West Virginia gas well, sending flames 200 feet into the sky as crowds gathered to witness one of America’s most extraordinary fires
Article Text:
Lightning ignited a massive West Virginia gas well, sending flames 200 feet into the sky (Image Credit: West Virginia Explorer)

A giant gas discovery

Lightning creates a giant flame

The fire blew itself out

In 1895, a lightning strike turned an already uncontrollable natural gas well in West Virginia into a spectacular column of fire. The Big Moses gas well, located along Indian Creek in Tyler County, had become famous after drillers searching for oil instead struck an enormous underground supply of natural gas. According to West Virginia Explorer, the well produced gas with such extraordinary pressure that efforts to contain it repeatedly failed. When lightning ignited the escaping gas on June 14, 1895, flames reportedly rose 150 to 200 feet into the air and attracted crowds from the surrounding countryside. However, historical newspaper accounts cited by various sources reveal an important detail often lost in later retellings: the lightning-triggered fire itself lasted only about two hours before the force of the escaping gas blew it out.The story of Big Moses began in 1894, during a major oil and gas boom in Tyler County. Drillers were searching for oil on the Moses Spencer farm near Sistersville when they struck the well on September 6. Instead of oil, they encountered an enormous flow of natural gas. The pressure was extraordinary. As per contemporary accounts, the force of the escaping gas was powerful enough to blow the drilling tools completely out of the hole and through the derrick.Estimates of the well's output varied considerably. Some historical accounts placed its initial flow at as much as 100 million cubic feet of gas per day, while a later federal estimate put it at about 35 million cubic feet per day. Whatever the exact figure, Big Moses was an exceptionally powerful well for its time and was widely regarded as one of the world's largest gas wells.The problem was that the technology available in the 1890s was not well suited to controlling such a high-pressure source. Workers repeatedly attempted to shut the well, but the gas continued to force its way out. At one point, the owners installed a massive casing weighing several tons. Although the effort initially appeared successful, sand and small stones propelled upward by the gas eventually damaged the casing and allowed the well to escape again. Another attempt involved pumping water into the well for five days. Instead of stopping the gas, the pressure forced water through cracks in the surrounding ground, reportedly creating numerous small geysers, some nearly half a mile from the well.As Big Moses continued releasing gas, it became both an industrial problem and a local spectacle. People travelled to see the enormous well, while newspapers described its deafening roar and the difficulty of standing close enough to speak normally. Then, on June 14, 1895, a thunderstorm passed through the area. Lightning struck the column of gas escaping from the well, igniting it almost instantly. The result was a spectacular blaze that illuminated the surrounding countryside. Various reports described the flames as reaching extraordinary heights, with one account putting them at between 150 and 200 feet. The fire appeared to create a new problem for the well's owners. They had already struggled to contain the gas, and now the escaping fuel was burning above the wellhead. Crowds gathered to witness the unusual spectacle. Newspapers described the scene as both frightening and remarkable, with the enormous flame visible from a considerable distance. But the fire did not continue indefinitely.Despite later stories suggesting that Big Moses burned for a year or even decades, the contemporary accounts tell a different story. The lightning-triggered blaze lasted only about two hours. The reason was almost as remarkable as the fire itself: the tremendous pressure of the escaping gas eventually blew the flames out. A June 18, 1895, report in the Parkersburg Daily Sentinel said the fire had burned for about two hours before the immense force of the gas extinguished flames that had been reaching an estimated 150 to 200 feet into the air. West Virginia's official historical archives preserve contemporary reports documenting both the lightning strike and the subsequent extinguishing of the blaze.Big Moses itself continued to be a major uncontrolled gas flow after the spectacular fire. Historical records indicate that the well ultimately stopped flowing on August 27, 1895, after months of attempts to control it. The episode became part of West Virginia's early oil-and-gas history because it demonstrated both the enormous energy stored beneath the region and the limitations of 19th-century drilling technology. Big Moses had been drilled in search of oil, but instead revealed a huge natural gas resource that engineers of the era struggled to harness. More than a century later, the well remains memorable not because its lightning fire lasted for decades, but because of the extraordinary sequence of events surrounding it: an enormous gas discovery, repeated failed attempts to control the pressure, a lightning strike that created a towering flame and, finally, a fire powerful enough to be extinguished by the very gas that had created it.
Article Summary: Lightning ignited a massive West Virginia gas well, sending flames 200 feet into the sky. The well, called Big Moses, had become famous after drillers searching for oil instead struck an enormous underground supply of natural gas. When lightning ignited the escaping gas on June 14, 1895, flames reportedly rose 150 to 200 feet in the air. However, historical newspaper accounts cited by various sources reveal an important detail often lost in later retellings: the lightning-triggered fire itself lasted only about two hours before the force of the escaped gas blew it out.

Article Title: Flight recorders recovered from Amazon cargo jet that overran Miami airport runway, killing five
Article Text:
NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy described the crash scene as "utterly devastation"

Federal investigators examining cause of deadly overrun

Investigators have recovered the flight and voice recorders from an Amazon cargo plane that overran the runway at Miami International Airport, killing five people, National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said Monday (local time).All five victims were in a van and an SUV that were among several vehicles struck by the jet outside airport property. The van was carrying seven people from a cleaning company.Homendy called the scene of Sunday’s crash “utter devastation.""It's (debris) pretty extensive. I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well. I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation,” Homendy said.The van, owned by airline cleaning contractor Professional Ocean Service Corp., was “torn apart,” she added.The NTSB will issue further information Tuesday (local time), potentially including the aircraft’s speed as confirmed by the flight data recorder.The incident also left three people critically injured and two others hospitalised with severe injuries.Investigators are examining whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.Video of the cargo jet's Sunday landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Investigators will seek to determine exactly where it landed, whether that was beyond the normal touchdown zone and why the pilots did not abort the landing.They will also examine the plane’s speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, mechanical condition and other factors that may have contributed to the crash.The aircraft flew from Cincinnati to Miami and then to San Juan, Puerto Rico, before returning to Miami. It overran the runway around 2 pm, crossing a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses surrounding the airport.The crash sent thick black smoke into the sky and trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit, while some people were trapped in vehicles. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue crews also had to free a person trapped beneath a vehicle.
Article Summary: Federal investigators examining cause of deadly overrun at Miami International Airport. NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy described the crash scene as "utterly devastation" The incident also left three people critically injured and two others hospitalised with severe injuries. Investigators are examining whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.

Article Title: 'Stop treating America like a piggybank': Trump threatens to block Canada's Bombardier jets in US
Article Text:
Trump threatens to stop sale of Canada's Bombardier jets

US President Donald Trump on Monday threatened to bar Canadian aircraft manufacturer Bombardier from selling its jets in the United States unless the company moves its manufacturing operations to American soil, escalating trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa.In a post on Truth Social, MAGA supremo Trump targeted the Montreal-based business jet maker, accusing Canada of pursuing protectionist policies against US companies."NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!" Trump wrote. "Over 50% of their revenue comes from the United States — They live off American Buyers, American Companies, American Airports, and American Service — All while Canada blocks our GREAT American Banks, and Companies, throughout the USA"Trump also accused Canadian authorities of restricting US aircraft manufacturer Gulfstream Aerospace from operating in Canada."They even blocked Gulfstream Aerospace from doing business in Canada — Completely unjust and unfair! That Era is OVER!" Trump added. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank.' BUY AMERICAN. FLY ON AMERICAN AIRLINERS. ENJOY AMERICAN LIQUOR AND BEVERAGES. SAIL ON LAKE AMERICA. AMERICA FIRST!"Trump's remarks come amid escalating trade tensions between the two North American neighbours following the breakdown of bilateral trade talks and threats of retaliatory tariffs on key goods.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier said Ottawa remained ready to negotiate a durable trade agreement with Washington while protecting Canadian workers, families and businesses."We are always going to stand up for what's in the best interest of Canada, Canadian workers, and Canadian families, not look for an easy win, not looking for an announcement, but something that's durable. And that deal is possible; that's in both of our benefits," Carney said at a press conference.Carney said a trade agreement benefiting Canadian workers, families and businesses would also serve the interests of American consumers, businesses and families.He also indicated that Canada would not simply wait for Washington to make the next move, saying Ottawa was working to strengthen its domestic economy and expand trade ties with other countries."It is talking to and concluding agreements with all the countries around the world who want to make a deal with Canada," Carney added.The Canadian leader reiterated that Ottawa had suspended trade negotiations with the US after rejecting terms proposed by Washington."Our country is being tested. Two weeks ago, we made the right decision to suspend our trade negotiations with the United States. We couldn't accept what they'd offered. We wouldn't give what they'd asked.
